response: HTTP/2 reduces head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer by multiplexing streams, but TCP still has transport-level head-of-line blocking: a lost packet can delay all streams sharing that connection. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, so loss generally affects only the relevant stream. It can also improve connection setup and connection migration, especially on mobile or lossy networks. HTTP/2 can still be a good choice where compatibility, infrastructure maturity, or operational simplicity matter.

I wouldn’t. One namespace and cluster-admin service accounts make early setup easy, but create a large blast radius: any compromised workload can potentially control the whole cluster. At minimum, use separate service accounts with least-privilege RBAC, keep production isolated from non-production, and split namespaces by environment and/or trust boundary. You can still keep the deployment workflow simple with templates or Helm/Kustomize.

It’s not pedantry; RAID 1 protects against a specific failure: a disk dying. A backup protects against many others: accidental deletion, corruption, ransomware, a bad deployment, theft, fire, or both disks/controller failing together. RAID can improve availability and reduce downtime, which is valuable, but it usually mirrors mistakes immediately. Use RAID if you need resilience, plus separate versioned backups tested for restore.

MongoDB is not inherently the standard choice for financial ledgers; many systems prefer relational databases because transactions, constraints, and auditability map naturally to ledger requirements. MongoDB can still work if its operational tradeoffs fit your system. Model each business event as an immutable transaction document with balanced debit and credit postings, amounts in integer minor units, currency, timestamps, account IDs, idempotency key, and audit metadata. Enforce that postings sum to zero in a database transaction, never mutate posted entries—use reversing entries—and maintain derived balances separately so they can be rebuilt from the ledger.

Kafka does not delete a record when a consumer reads it. Records are retained according to topic retention policies, and each consumer group tracks its own offset. Put the two services in different consumer groups; each group will receive and process every event independently. If they are in the same group, Kafka distributes partitions among them for load balancing, so each record goes to only one group member.

Usually, no. Finishing a full draft before sharing can work if you need privacy or a private exploratory draft, but it risks investing heavily in a structure or voice that readers do not respond to. Share a strong early chapter or a short outline with a few trusted target readers, ask focused questions, and use the feedback to course-correct. Keep writing while feedback is coming in so outside opinions don’t stall momentum.

The 200k matters for learning and accountability, but unless you can recover it by stopping, it should not determine whether to continue. The decision is: from today onward, is the expected value of spending the additional money and time better than the best alternative use of those resources? Finishing may absolutely be right—but because the remaining investment has a credible payoff, not because past spending obligates you to add more.

Standups are not universally a waste of time. They can be useful when they are brief, focused on coordination, and solve real blockers; they become wasteful when they turn into status theater. If your team does not need synchronous daily coordination, replace them with an async written update covering progress, next steps, blockers, and requests for help, plus a short ad hoc coordination meeting only when needed. Try it for a few weeks and measure whether blockers are surfaced quickly and meetings decrease.
